  Readable gloss: "A noun saturating the prophetic books -- Jeremiah alone uses it twenty-four times. It oscillates between two poles: the objective state of ruin (a land lying waste) and the subjective reaction of horror in those who witness it. Psalm 46:9 pictures God making 'desolations' in the earth, while Deuteronomy 28:37 warns Israel will become an object of 'horror' among the nations. German 'Entsetzen' (dismay) gravitates toward the emotional pole; Spanish 'desolacion' sits closer to the physical. The formulaic curse 'for a desolation and a hissing' (Jer 19:8; 25:9, 18) fuses both dimensions into a single devastating image."

  Sense 1: "desolation, waste (state of ruin)"
    Enriched: The objective sense of physical desolation: a place reduced to waste and ruin. Psalm 46:8 envisions God's cosmic 'desolations,' and Isaiah 5:9 prophesies houses becoming 'a waste.' Jeremiah's oracles frequently deploy this in the lamed-of-result construction -- 'I will make this city a desolation' (Jer 4:7; 51:29, 43). German 'Entsetzen' slightly overstates the emotional; Spanish 'desolacion' bett...
    Existing Spanish translations: desolación, en-desolación, para-desolación, por-desolación
  Sense 2: "horror, object of appalment"
    Enriched: The subjective sense: something that provokes horror and shocked dismay in onlookers. Deuteronomy 28:37 warns Israel will become 'a horror' among the peoples, and Jeremiah 5:30 declares 'a horrible thing has happened in the land.' The prophetic curse formula pairs this with 'hissing' and 'reproach' (Jer 18:16; 19:8; 25:9, 18), marking communities that provoke shuddering dread.
    Existing Spanish translations: Cosa-espantosa, como-desolación, desolación, en-horror, horror, para-desolación, para-horror, por-horror, y-a-horror, y-por-espanto
  Sense 3: "become desolate (Niphal)"
    Enriched: A single Niphal verbal occurrence (Zech 7:14) where the land 'was made desolate' behind the exiles. Unlike the nominal senses describing a state or an emotional reaction, this captures the process of becoming ruined -- the transition from inhabited to waste. Spanish 'quedo desolada' and the German bracketed form both reflect the verbal-processual character.
    Existing Spanish translations: quedó-desolada
